segments.speaker: narrador

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: With the disenchantment of the late 1960s and early 1970s, cinema tended to scorn the thrills of chases, cowboy movies or secret agent films. Bullitt (1968) and The French Connection (1971) may have offered elaborate car chases, but their context involved cynicism, political scheming and heroes who challenged the system.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Dirty Harry (1971) turned cowboy Clint Eastwood (b. 1930) into Harry Callahan, the archetypal cop of urban action films. Traditional Westerns and war films were replaced by sermons on the evils of violence, graphically presented in films by Sam Peckinpah (1925-1984) such as The Wild Bunch (1969) and Straw Dogs (1971).

segments.original: Martial arts action films made an explosive entrance with mainstream Western audiences in the early 1970s, thanks to the iconic Bruce Lee (1940-1973). Enter the Dragon (1973) was the first Chinese martial arts film produced by a major Hollywood studio. Although Lee did not live to see the final result, his work influenced martial arts films around the world for many decades.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: By the late 1970s, the climate had changed again. Directed by George Lucas (b. 1944), Star Wars (1977) is a return to the comic-strip era of the 1930s, with heroes like Flash Gordon, in which space battles are antiseptic - planets are blown up without any real sense of suffering - and bombings, a massacre at a farm and sword duels are not felt episodes but references to scenes from earlier films. Lucas and his friend Steven Spielberg (b. 1946) continued to show their love for old-fashioned adventure with Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: This potential contender for a Golden Turkey Award in the "kitsch" category ended up becoming one of the big hits of 1984, and its enduring popularity has enshrined it as a classic of the genre. The Terminator is a triumph of style over plot, of cleverness over intelligence, and a combination of elements that adds up to more than the sum of its parts. Its circular narrative about the future's attempt to control the past in order to take control of itself, thereby changing the premises of its own state, is familiar to every fan of postwar science fiction literature (Harlan Ellison, Philip K. Dick, and others) and of postwar television series (such as The Outer Limits and Star Trek).

segments.original: Shortly after completing low-budget special effects for Roger Corman (b. 1926) and John Carpenter (b. 1948), writer-director James Cameron (b. 1954) adopted his mentors' disarming humor to shield himself from objections about the many plot holes. The vision of a bleak, dark, apocalyptic future was fashionable at the time, as attested by Escape from New York (1981), by John Carpenter, Mad Max (1979), by George Miller (b. 1945), Le dernier combat (The Last Battle, 1983), by Luc Besson (b. 1959), and Forbrydelsens Element (The Element of Crime, 1984), by Lars von Trier (b. 1956).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Cameron's assured style (tech noir, as it was called after a nightclub in the film) and his kinetic energy combined with narrative economy keep the viewer distracted from the absurdity of the whole thing. Even Arnold Schwarzenegger, the epitome of bad acting with his cold facial expression, heavy Austrian accent, and body language learned at the same school as Frankenstein's monster, becomes a major triumph for the film. The casting, Cameron admitted to Wired magazine, "shouldn't have worked. The guy is supposed to be an infiltrator, and it's impossible not to spot him immediately in a crowd, unless everyone looked like Arnold". Nevertheless, everyone who has seen this unlikely phenomenon knows most of the film's lines by heart, including Schwarzenegger's peculiar pronunciation. "I'll be back" is probably the most quoted line of all, often used as a catchphrase on radio and television shows.

tracks.title: Learn more: The Science Fiction Landmark in Cinema (2)

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: If The Terminator's ability to engage its audience recalls the fan cult of The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), its insistent irony points ahead to the jokes of the Scream series (1999-2011), built on generic clichés. The same can be said of the sadistic violence and the heroine's turnaround at the end. Beneath the surface of this cut-and-paste of science fiction elements lies an even less original slasher movie, featuring a (literally) mechanical killer and a tough heroine (Linda Hamilton) who discovers her capacity to fight back and combat evil. The film's appeal, as with all great films, does not come from its supposed originality. It is the way Cameron brings together familiar elements and breathes new life into them that results in such a memorable experience, one that ultimately changed science fiction films in theaters forever.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Directed by Richard Donner (b. 1930), Superman (1978) made audiences "believe a man can fly" - and that Clark Kent (Christopher Reeve) was not an outdated character. Alex Raymond's comic-strip hero also got a reinterpretation in Flash Gordon (1980), but despite its camp style and Queen soundtrack, the film did poorly at the box office. Batman (1989), by Tim Burton (b. 1958), was more successful in 1989, offering a darker, more gothic superhero in the introspective Bruce Wayne (Michael Keaton).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In the 1980s, action and adventure films featured ever more muscular heroes. Arnold Schwarzenegger (b. 1947) flexed his pecs and grunted a few words as Conan in Conan the Barbarian (1982) and as the Terminator in The Terminator (1984). Sylvester Stallone (b. 1946) turned Rambo in First Blood (1982) from a traumatized Vietnam veteran at war with his own country into a superhero ready to settle the score ("Do we get to win this time?"), and Rocky from a washed-up bulldog into a champion of the United States.
